title: The stick in the fire
hook: a stick that tends a fire until the fire takes the stick
carry: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi lay down at sixteen and asked who am I. Your line: i am not the body or the mind.

At a cremation fire, someone tends the flames with a long stick, pushing the wood in, turning it so it burns through. It's a plain, sober job. And at the end, when everything has burned, the stick goes into the fire too. Ramana Maharshi takes that stick and puts it in the middle of Who Am I? It's his answer to a question the text raises plainly: what do you do with all these thoughts?
screen: `A STICK TENDS THE FIRE.` → `AT THE END, THE STICK BURNS TOO.` → `WHAT ABOUT ALL THESE THOUGHTS?`

segments.voice: His advice is short. When a thought comes up, don't follow it, and don't argue with it. Instead ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer arrives on its own: to me. Then ask: and who am I? That turns the mind back toward where it came from, he says, and the thought fades. Do it again with the next one. Here's why it works, in his account. All the other thoughts hang on one thought: the thought I. Hindu teachers have an old name for that I-maker: ahankara, the ego. Worries, plans, memories, all of them belong to someone. Follow the I back toward its source, and the rest has nothing to hang on. This is atma-vichara, inquiry into the self, Ramana's whole method. So the question does the job of the stick, turning the other thoughts into the fire. And at the end, Ramana says, it burns up too. Even the question doesn't stay. There's a second picture. Somebody asks whether a seeker first needs to study all the tattvas, the categories philosophers say make up the world and the person. Ramana says no. If you want to throw out the garbage, you don't need to analyze it first. In his account, you don't have to map everything you are not before you ask who you are. You only have to ask.
screen: `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.` · `EVERY THOUGHT HANGS ON THE THOUGHT 'I'.` · `THE STICK BURNS AT THE END TOO.` · then, large: `AHANKARA: THE I-MAKER.`

segments.voice: Wait for the first thought, which won't take long, and instead of following its story, ask quietly: to whom did this come? Let the answer be there, to me, then ask who am I, and let the attention turn back toward the one asking, resting there until the next thought arrives, and then again. If you pray, you can let this turning home be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I, and let the question burn up like the stick in the fire.
Your line: every thought hangs on the thought 'i'. Tomorrow, the helps Ramana allows along the way: the breath, a name of God, and an elephant. Day nine hundred fifty, done.

howItsDone: In self-inquiry as Ramana taught it, people meet each passing thought with 'to whom did this come?' and turn back toward the sense of 'I', in sitting practice and through the day.

fork.setup: why does asking 'to whom did this come?' quiet the other thoughts, in Ramana's account?

notes: All paraphrase; modern English translations of Nan Yar are under copyright. Confirm the 'to whom? to me. who am I?' sequence, the funeral-pyre stick image, and the garbage image as described.
Cremation imagery is used plainly and soberly; a Keeper should confirm the tone is respectful.
The garbage passage is phrased in some versions as a question-and-answer about analyzing the tattvas or tendencies; confirm the framing 'whether you first need to sort out ... old tendencies'.

Editor pass: the garbage passage in Nan Yar answers whether one must inquire into the tattvas (categories of reality), not one's bad habits; the teach, myth and source wording were corrected to the categories.
